chapterBreakdown.gentle:
A team can admire its strengths and still weaken its strategy. It says it has talented people, strong execution, and good habits, so it assumes the strategy should fit whatever those strengths already are. The chapter pushes back on that comfort. A strength matters strategically only when it helps the company deliver the chosen edge on the chosen field.

Gillette gives the chapter its clearest example. The case matters because it shows that a strategic edge depends on what the organization can repeatedly do well, not just on what it wants customers to believe. That is the chapter's useful lesson. Capabilities are not a list of proud traits. They are the things the strategy needs in order to work.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
Capabilities are the strategic choice about what the organization must be distinctly good at to make its chosen edge real. Without that fit, how to win remains only a promise. The chapter argues that strengths do not deserve strategic importance simply because they already exist.

Gillette works here because it makes capability fit concrete. The chapter's point is not to celebrate talent in the abstract. It is to show that the strategy has to be backed by reinforcing abilities that actually deliver the value it claims.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
A company can be proud of the wrong strengths for years. It can call them assets, heritage, or excellence and still use them to avoid a harder strategic question: do these capabilities actually support the field and edge we chose? The chapter's correction is brutal. If the strengths do not fit the game, they are drag.

Gillette is the proof case. The case matters because it shows that the edge lives in what the organization can repeatedly make happen, not in what it likes saying about itself. A chosen edge with no matching capability set is still a bluff.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
Teams often say they are playing to their strengths when they really mean they are admiring what they already know how to do. That language can sound disciplined because it favors what is familiar and proven. The problem is that a strength is not automatically strategic. It only matters if it helps the company deliver the edge it chose on the field it chose. When that fit is missing, the organization may be protecting an impressive skill set that actually pulls attention away from the strategy.

Capabilities follow how to win because a chosen edge is still only a promise until the organization can make it real. The next question is not what the company happens to be proud of. It is what the company must be distinctly good at for the strategy to hold. The chapter insists on that difference. Capabilities are not a loose inventory of talents. They are the critical things the organization must do well if its chosen field and edge are going to survive contact with reality.

Gillette gives the chapter its clearest anchor because it shows capability fit as a strategic issue rather than a slogan about strengths. The chapter then widens the lesson through activity-system logic. One strong function rarely rescues a weak system. What matters is a reinforcing set of actions and abilities that strengthen one another in service of the edge. That is why the chapter also keeps a limit visible. A company can become extremely capable in the wrong direction. If the capabilities do not fit the strategy, then even disciplined strength becomes expensive drag.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
Capabilities are the strategic answer to a practical question: what must the organization be able to do better than a generic competitor in order to make its chosen edge hold? Teams blur that question when they treat strengths as inherently valuable. The chapter rejects that move. A strength only matters if it supports the chosen field and the chosen how-to-win logic.

This is why capabilities arrive after how to win in the cascade. A company cannot know which capabilities matter until it has already chosen the game and the basis of preference inside that game. Once those choices are clear, the capability question becomes sharper. What abilities, processes, and reinforcing actions must exist for that edge to be credible? The chapter refuses generic talent language because a strategy is not served by every strength equally.

Gillette is the chapter's main anchor because it makes capability fit concrete without widening into unsupported detail. The deeper lesson is about reinforcement. An activity system matters more than one admired function because the edge has to be delivered through coordinated action, not isolated excellence. The chapter therefore pushes against two mistakes at once: admiring strengths that do not fit the strategy and believing one strong node can compensate for a weak system. It also preserves the harder limit. A company can build real capability and still support the wrong game. When that happens, the strength becomes strategically misdirected rather than useful.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
A lot of companies protect their favorite strengths the way other companies protect their favorite markets. They call those strengths world class, proven, or part of the firm's identity, then assume strategy should bend around them. The chapter cuts into that vanity. If the capability does not support the field and edge you chose, then the capability is not a strategic asset. It is an expensive habit.

Capabilities matter because how to win is still fiction until the organization can repeatedly deliver it. That is the real question here. What does the company need to be able to do so the edge is more than a sentence? The chapter refuses a generic talent inventory because most strengths are only conditionally valuable. Their value depends on whether they reinforce the actual game the company says it is playing.

Gillette is the useful anchor because it keeps the chapter tied to capability fit instead of drifting into motivational language. The sharper lesson comes from the activity system idea. One strong function does not save a weak strategy any more than one good player saves a broken team design. The edge lives in reinforcement across the system. That is why the chapter is also ruthless about the limit. A company can become extremely capable in a direction that no longer matters strategically. When that happens, discipline becomes drag and excellence becomes misallocation.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
The chapter's hardest correction is that strengths are easy to admire and hard to judge strategically. A company can point to skilled teams, proven routines, respected expertise, and disciplined execution, then feel reassured that it is building on solid ground. But reassurance is not the same as fit. A strength only matters strategically when it supports the chosen field and the chosen edge. Otherwise the company may be protecting something impressive that is no longer helping it win.

Capabilities matter because how to win is still only a promise until the organization can repeatedly deliver it. The chapter asks a sharper question than self-description. What must this company be distinctly good at for its chosen game to work? That is why capabilities follow how to win in the cascade. The strategy chooses the game first. Then it chooses the delivery power that makes the game credible. A long list of admirable strengths is useless if it does not answer that question.

Gillette gives the argument its clearest shape because the case keeps capability fit visible without inviting unsupported detail. The useful lesson is not acquisition theater. It is that a strategic edge depends on repeatable organizational ability, not on hope, pride, or broad talent language. The case matters because it makes capability fit feel structural rather than inspirational.

The chapter then rejects another comforting simplification. Capabilities do not work as isolated skills. One strong function rarely rescues a weak system. What matters is an activity system: a reinforcing set of actions, processes, and abilities that strengthen one another in service of the edge. When that system fits, the strategy starts to feel coherent even under pressure. When it does not, one strong node compensates for several weak ones and the company mistakes strain for strength.

The chapter is also stricter than generic strengths advice because it refuses loyalty to legacy strengths. Existing capabilities do not deserve protection simply because they were expensive to build or once made the company proud. If they do not support the chosen field and edge, then they have become drag. The useful question is not what the company is good at in the abstract. It is what this strategy requires the company to be good at now.

That keeps the real limit visible. A company can become highly capable in the wrong direction. It can assemble disciplined teams, reinforcing activities, and genuine expertise that all work beautifully together, yet still be supporting a weak edge or the wrong game. Capabilities only count strategically when they fit the whole choice cascade. The next chapter matters because once the capability set is chosen, the company still has to ask what systems will keep it reinforced instead of letting it decay.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
Capabilities are the strategic choice about what the organization must be able to do distinctively well in order to make its chosen edge hold. Teams often blur that by treating strengths as inherently valuable. The chapter rejects that shortcut. A strength is not strategic because it exists. It becomes strategic only when it supports the chosen field and the chosen how-to-win logic.

This is why capabilities arrive after how to win. A company cannot know which capabilities matter until it has already chosen the game and the basis of preference inside that game. Once those choices are in place, the capability question becomes specific. What set of repeatable abilities, processes, and reinforcing actions must exist for the edge to be credible? The chapter's discipline lies in strategic necessity, not in self-esteem.

Gillette is the chapter's anchor because it makes capability fit concrete without needing unsupported expansion. The lesson is that an edge depends on what the organization can repeatedly deliver. That is what turns strategy from a persuasive story into an operational claim. Capability fit is therefore part of the edge itself, not merely implementation support attached later.

The activity-system logic sharpens that lesson. One admired function does not save a weak system because the edge has to be delivered through reinforcement. Capabilities matter as a set of mutually strengthening actions, not as isolated pockets of excellence. When the system fits, strengths compound. When the system does not fit, the organization pays hidden coordination costs and starts calling those costs commitment.

The limit matters as much as the correction. Existing strengths are not entitled to strategic loyalty. A company can build genuine capability and still support the wrong field or the wrong edge. In that case excellence becomes misallocated rather than useful. The chapter is strongest where it keeps that discomfort alive: strengths deserve investment only when they reinforce the actual strategy. Once that fit is named, the next question becomes inevitable. What systems will protect those reinforcing capabilities from drift, decay, and internal contradiction?
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
The easiest way to fake strategic discipline in this chapter is to confuse pride with fit. A company says it has great people, world-class functions, proven processes, and elite execution, then acts as if strategy should naturally bend around those assets. The chapter cuts against that vanity. If the strengths do not support the field and edge you chose, then they are not strategic assets. They are expensive habits with better public relations.

Capabilities matter because a chosen edge is still fiction until the organization can repeatedly deliver it. That is the real question here. What must this company be able to do so the edge survives contact with reality? The chapter refuses generic talent language because most strengths are only conditionally useful. Their value depends on whether they reinforce the actual game the company says it is playing.

Gillette is the chapter's model because it keeps the argument tied to capability fit instead of drifting into motivational talk. The case shows that the edge lives in what the organization can make happen over and over, not in what it hopes the market will infer. That is why capabilities are not decorative support. They are part of the win condition.

The activity-system idea makes the chapter harsher. One brilliant function does not rescue a broken system any more than one star player rescues a team with the wrong design. The edge has to live across reinforcing actions. If one node keeps compensating for several weak ones, the company starts mistaking strain for proof of character. Really it is paying for design failure.

The chapter also refuses nostalgia for legacy strengths. A capability can be real, rare, and deeply admired and still be strategically wrong for the game now being played. That is the painful limit. Excellence becomes drag when it reinforces the wrong direction. Capabilities earn their status only when they fit the cascade from field, to edge, to reinforcement. After that, one more pressure remains. The company has to build systems that keep those capabilities from fragmenting back into isolated effort.

examples.title: Mira's Team Lists Capabilities It Cannot Yet Prove

scenario.gentle: Mira stands by a whiteboard covered with capabilities her team says it needs to win: premium service, flawless delivery, deep analytics, and trusted relationships. The list looks impressive, but half of it feels aspirational rather than real.
scenario.direct: Mira's team is naming the right-sounding capabilities without testing whether the organization can actually deliver them yet.
scenario.competitive: Mira is staring at capability theater: a strategy pretending the delivery power already exists.

whatToDo.gentle: Separate the capabilities the team can already demonstrate from the ones it is only hoping to have, then rebuild the plan around that gap honestly.
whatToDo.direct: Turn the whiteboard into a fit audit. Identify which required capabilities are real, which are weak, and which would need investment before the edge can be credible.
whatToDo.competitive: Stop treating aspiration like delivery power. Name the gaps before the market does.

whyItMatters.gentle: A strategy gets fragile when it depends on capabilities the organization does not really have yet.
whyItMatters.direct: Capability claims that outrun operational reality usually turn the chosen edge into a promise the company cannot keep.
whyItMatters.competitive: Fake delivery power is how a good-looking edge dies in public.

examples.title: Jonah Learns That Polish Was Not the Needed Strength

scenario.gentle: Jonah's case competition team gets praised for polished slides and strong speaking, but the judges keep asking whether the recommendation can actually be delivered by the organization described in the case.
scenario.direct: Jonah's team is admiring presentation strength while missing the capabilities required by the recommended strategy.
scenario.competitive: Jonah just found out that polish is not the same thing as strategic fit.

whatToDo.gentle: Rework the recommendation around the few capabilities the organization would truly need to make the edge real, even if the presentation becomes less flashy.
whatToDo.direct: Shift the analysis from admired team strengths to the capability system required by the proposed strategy.
whatToDo.competitive: Stop winning the room and losing the logic. Build the answer around delivery fit.

whyItMatters.gentle: A team can look strong and still ignore the real capability question.
whyItMatters.direct: The wrong admired strength can distract attention from whether the strategy is actually executable.
whyItMatters.competitive: If the strength serves the presentation instead of the strategy, it is camouflage.

examples.title: Aileen Stops Treating Enthusiasm as a Capability Set

scenario.gentle: Aileen tells a friend her side project will work because she is disciplined, creative, and willing to learn fast. Her friend asks which specific abilities the project actually depends on.
scenario.direct: Aileen is describing admirable traits, but she has not translated them into the few capabilities her chosen offer truly requires.
scenario.competitive: Aileen has energy and identity, but not yet a capability system.

whatToDo.gentle: Name the small set of abilities the project must have to deliver its promise, then stop treating every positive trait as equally strategic.
whatToDo.direct: Convert the personal strengths list into a fit test: what does the edge require, what can she already do, and what still needs building?
whatToDo.competitive: Cut the self-description. Build the few capabilities the edge actually needs.

whyItMatters.gentle: A project becomes clearer when strengths are filtered by strategic fit instead of personal pride.
whyItMatters.direct: Not every admirable trait deserves equal investment if the strategy depends on only a few capabilities.
whyItMatters.competitive: Identity is not an edge until it turns into repeatable delivery power.

examples.title: Omar Finds the One Strong Node in a Weak System

scenario.gentle: Omar reviews a process map and sees one exceptional customer-success team carrying three sloppy handoffs upstream and downstream. Everyone keeps praising the one strong team for saving the strategy.
scenario.direct: Omar's company has one admired capability node, but the surrounding system is too weak to reinforce the chosen edge consistently.
scenario.competitive: Omar found the pattern: one elite function is compensating for a broken design.

whatToDo.gentle: Ask what reinforcing actions around that strong team are missing, then fix the system instead of only celebrating the hero function.
whatToDo.direct: Treat the process map as an activity-system problem. The edge needs coordinated capabilities, not one compensating star.
whatToDo.competitive: Stop worshipping the rescue team. Repair the cold nodes that keep draining the edge.

whyItMatters.gentle: A strategy can look alive because one function keeps absorbing the strain.
whyItMatters.direct: Isolated excellence usually hides system weakness rather than solving it.
whyItMatters.competitive: One hot node can mask a dead system long enough to create false confidence.

examples.title: Tessa Questions the Club's Favorite Legacy Strength

scenario.gentle: Tessa leads a student entrepreneurship club that is proud of its event-planning strength, even though the club now says it wants to win by producing deeper startup coaching. The old strength still dominates every meeting.
scenario.direct: Tessa's club is protecting a legacy strength that no longer fits the edge it claims to be pursuing.
scenario.competitive: Tessa can see the club bending the new strategy around an old capability it does not want to demote.

whatToDo.gentle: Ask whether the favorite strength still supports the club's chosen edge or whether it now pulls time and energy in the wrong direction.
whatToDo.direct: Re-rank the club's capabilities by strategic fit instead of tradition, then stop treating legacy excellence as untouchable.
whatToDo.competitive: Cut the nostalgia tax. If the old strength serves the wrong game, it loses priority.

whyItMatters.gentle: A proud legacy capability can quietly trap a team in yesterday's strategy.
whyItMatters.direct: Strategic fit matters more than inherited competence once the edge changes.
whyItMatters.competitive: Legacy strength becomes strategic drag when identity outranks fit.

examples.title: Rohan Wins More by Building Fewer, Tighter Capabilities

scenario.gentle: Rohan has been trying to build every useful freelance skill at once. Progress feels slow until he narrows to a smaller set of abilities that reinforce one another and fit the offer he actually wants to sell.
scenario.direct: Rohan's first approach scattered effort across too many strengths. The reset works because the capabilities now reinforce a specific edge.
scenario.competitive: Rohan stops collecting talents and starts building a capability system.

whatToDo.gentle: Choose the few abilities that directly support the offer and strengthen one another, then let the rest wait.

whatToDo.competitive: Stack the capabilities that sharpen the edge. Ignore the vanity extras for now.

front.gentle: What is the chapter's warning about strengths?
front.direct: How can a highly capable organization still be strategically weak?

back.gentle: A company can become strong in the wrong direction if its capabilities do not fit the strategy.
back.direct: Capabilities become misallocated strength when they reinforce the wrong field or edge instead of the chosen one.
back.competitive: Excellence becomes drag when it keeps making the company better at the wrong game.

keyTakeawayCard.gentle: The chapter turns strengths into a harder test: do they help deliver the chosen edge? They only count strategically when they fit the field, the edge, and the reinforcing system around them.
keyTakeawayCard.direct: The chapter defines capabilities through fit and reinforcement rather than admiration. Without the right capability system, the edge remains only a promise.
keyTakeawayCard.competitive: Stop confusing proud strengths with strategic power. The edge gets real only when the right capabilities reinforce the right game.

questions.prompt: What do capabilities mean in this chapter?
choices: The things the organization must do well to make the edge real
Every strength the company has ever built
The traits leaders admire most in themselves

explanation.gentle: The chapter defines capabilities by what the strategy needs, not by pride or history.
explanation.direct: Capabilities are the distinct abilities required to deliver the chosen edge on the chosen field.
explanation.competitive: The right answer names delivery power. The others only describe vanity or inventory.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter use Gillette?
choices: To prove that any acquisition automatically creates capabilities
To show that strategic edge depends on capability fit
To argue that legacy strengths should never be questioned

explanation.gentle: Gillette matters because it shows that the edge depends on what the organization can repeatedly do.
explanation.direct: The anchor demonstrates that capability fit is part of the strategy itself rather than an optional support layer.
explanation.competitive: Gillette works here because delivery fit beats pride language.

questions.prompt: A team keeps praising a legacy strength that does not support its current edge. What is the clearest diagnosis?
choices: The team is wisely preserving all excellence equally
The team is protecting a misfit capability instead of testing strategic fit
The team has already solved the capability question

explanation.gentle: A real strength can still be wrong for the current strategy.
explanation.direct: This is admiration without fit. The team is keeping a capability central even though it no longer supports the chosen game.
explanation.competitive: They are funding pride instead of the edge.

questions.prompt: Mira's whiteboard lists capabilities the team hopes it has but cannot yet prove. What should happen next?
choices: Treat the whole list as real so momentum stays high
Separate the real capabilities from the gaps before promising the edge
Add more aspirational capabilities to make the plan complete

explanation.gentle: The team needs to tell the difference between current delivery power and future aspiration.
explanation.direct: A capability-fit audit should identify which required capabilities already exist and which still need investment.
explanation.competitive: Stop selling imagined delivery power. Name the gaps before the market does.

questions.prompt: What is the best distinction between admired strength and strategic capability?
choices: Admired strength is broader, while strategic capability is defined by fit to the chosen field and edge
Strategic capability always means the newest skill in the company
There is no difference if the team is confident

explanation.gentle: The chapter judges strength by whether it helps this strategy work.
explanation.direct: Strategic capability is narrower because it is defined by necessity and fit rather than general admiration.
explanation.competitive: Confidence does not create fit. The game does.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter emphasize an activity system?
choices: Because one admired function is usually enough by itself
Because capabilities need reinforcement across coordinated actions
Because systems make strategic choices unnecessary

explanation.gentle: The chapter wants capabilities to reinforce one another rather than stand alone.
explanation.direct: An activity system matters because the edge must be delivered through coordinated capabilities rather than isolated strengths.
explanation.competitive: One hot node cannot carry a cold system forever.

questions.prompt: Aileen lists disciplined, creative, and fast-learning as reasons her project will work. What is still missing?
choices: A clearer set of capabilities the offer actually requires
A longer list of admirable personal traits
A way to avoid choosing any specific capabilities

explanation.gentle: The project still needs a small set of abilities that directly support the chosen offer.
explanation.direct: She has described admirable traits, but not the capability set required by the edge she wants to build.
explanation.competitive: Identity is not yet delivery power. Fit still has to be named.

questions.prompt: Omar finds one elite customer-success team carrying several weak handoffs. What is the best next move?
choices: Celebrate the hero team and leave the rest alone
Repair the wider activity system instead of relying on one compensating node
Reduce attention to the strong team so the weak parts feel less exposed

explanation.gentle: The strong team is valuable, but the system still needs reinforcement around it.
explanation.direct: One strong function does not solve a system problem. The edge needs coordinated capabilities across the process.
explanation.competitive: Stop worshipping the rescue team and fix the dead nodes draining the strategy.

questions.prompt: What is the chapter's main limit on strengths advice?
choices: Every existing strength should dictate the strategy
A company can become highly capable in the wrong direction
Only weak organizations need capabilities

explanation.gentle: A strength still has to fit the chosen strategy before it counts as an asset.
explanation.direct: The chapter warns that real capability can still become misallocated when it supports the wrong field or edge.
explanation.competitive: Wrong-game excellence is still a strategic loss.

questions.prompt: Once the right capability set is clear, what question does the next chapter naturally raise?
choices: How can the company avoid measuring or reviewing those capabilities?
What systems will keep those capabilities reinforced over time?
How can the strategy stop depending on any capabilities at all?

explanation.gentle: Capabilities still need systems that keep them alive and coherent.
explanation.direct: The next strategic step is to identify the routines, measures, and management systems that reinforce the chosen capabilities.
explanation.competitive: Once the capability set is named, the system that keeps it from splintering becomes the next test.
